From the Penny Black to the Emoji

A Every evening Madina, a student in Seoul, records a voice message for her grandmother in Fergana, and her grandmother usually replies with a photo of her garden. Keeping in touch is so easy today that we forget how new it is.

B In Britain before 1840, the person who received a letter usually paid for it, and the price depended on the distance. Then a teacher called Rowland Hill had a simple idea: the sender pays, and a letter costs one penny to anywhere in the country. In May 1840 the first stamp, the Penny Black, appeared, and soon ordinary people were writing far more letters than before.

C In 1971 an American engineer, Ray Tomlinson, sent the first email between two computers on a network. The two computers were standing next to each other in the same room. Tomlinson chose the @ sign to separate the person's name from the computer's name, and we still use it in every email address.

D On 3 December 1992 a 22-year-old engineer, Neil Papworth, sent the first text message. He typed “Merry Christmas” on a computer and sent it to the phone of a Vodafone director. Phones at that time had no way to write messages, so the director couldn't reply.

E In 1999 a Japanese designer, Shigetaka Kurita, drew 176 tiny pictures for mobile phones — the first emoji. Each one was only 12 × 12 pixels, but they helped people to show feelings in very short messages. In 2016 the Museum of Modern Art in New York added them to its collection.

F So are we closer to more people today? Not really, says the Oxford scientist Robin Dunbar. His research suggests that we can keep about 150 meaningful relationships, and only about five very close ones — and social media hasn't changed these numbers. We are sending more messages than ever, but our hearts are the same size.

2

Grammar · present simple and present continuous

TUSHUNTIRISH — PRESENT SIMPLE VA PRESENT CONTINUOUS

A Present Simple — odatlar va kundalik ishlar uchun: I check my messages every morning. — va doimiy holatlar hamda hislar uchun: My grandmother lives in Fergana. She loves voice messages. Inkor va soʻroqda do / does: She doesn't use Instagram. · Do you write letters?

B Present Continuous (am / is / are + -ing) — hozir boʻlayotgan ishlar: Shh! I'm recording a message. — va shu kunlardagi vaqtinchalik ishlar: This year my brother is studying in Seoul. · More people are sending voice messages these days. be ni tushirib qoldirmang: She's watching — She watching emas.

C Vaqt soʻzlari: Simple — always, usually, every day, on Sundays · Continuous — now, at the moment, today, this week, these days. -ing imlosi: write → writing · chat → chatting · travel → travelling · lie → lying.

D Istisno — holat feʼllari. like, love, hate, want, need, know, understand, believe, prefer, mean, belong odatda Continuous da ishlatilmaydi: I know her — I'm knowing her emas. Ikki feʼlning maʼnosi oʻzgaradi: I think it's a good app (fikr) / I'm thinking about it (harakat) · I have a phone (egalik) / I'm having dinner (harakat).

DIQQAT — KOʻP UCHRAYDIGAN XATOLAR

1 ✗ I am liking this app. → ✓ I like this app. — like holat feʼli.

2 ✗ She watching a video now. → ✓ She's watching … — be ni tushirib qoldirmang.

3 ✗ He don't use social media. → ✓ He doesn't use … — he / she / it + doesn't.

4 ✗ I'm usually sending my mum a text at lunch. → ✓ I usually send … — bu odat.

5 ✗ What do you do now? Can I call you? → ✓ What are you doing now? — hozir boʻlayotgan ish.

6 ✗ Sorry, I'm not understanding your message. → ✓ I don't understand … — holat feʼli.

Vocabulary · adverbs and keeping in touch

3.1 Read Jasur's post. Look at the adverbs in bold.

Jasurning postini oʻqing. Qalin yozilgan ravishlarga qarang.

ME AND MY PHONE

I usually check my messages before breakfast — almost always on Telegram. I really like voice messages, especially from my grandmother, because I can hear her voice. I rarely make phone calls, and I hardly ever send emails — only to my teachers. I'm pretty good at replying quickly, but my brother is fairly slow: he sometimes answers the next day! I absolutely love sending photos, and I particularly enjoy getting photos of my cousin's new baby. My family lives in three different cities, but we keep in touch every day.

5

Writing · an email to someone you don't often see

TUSHUNTIRISH — YOZGANINGIZNI TEKSHIRING

A Tinish belgilari (P): savoldan keyin soʻroq belgisi · qisqa shakllarda apostrof: I'm, it's, what's, don't.

B Bosh harflar (C): ismlar, shahar va davlatlar, tillar va millatlar, hafta kunlari va oylar hamda I: Laylo, Almaty, Kazakh, Monday, July.

C Grammatika (G): he / she / it dan keyin -s · Present Continuous da be · savollarda soʻz tartibi.

D Imlo (Sp): usually · really · beautiful · friend · because · studying. Har bir xatni yuborishdan oldin toʻrttalasini tekshiring.

MODEL — AN EMAIL

Subject: Greetings from Almaty!

Dear Aunt Nodira and Uncle Rustam,

1 Hope you're both well. Sorry I didn't write last week — the days here are very busy!

2 As you know, I'm spending four weeks at a summer science camp in Almaty. The camp is in the mountains, and the views are absolutely gorgeous. This week we're studying plants and doing experiments in the lab.

3 Every day starts at seven. We usually have lessons in the morning, and in the afternoon we go walking or swimming. I hardly ever use my phone here, because there's no time!

4 There are forty students from six countries, so we always speak English together. My best friend here is Aigerim from Astana. She's teaching me some Kazakh words, and I'm teaching her Uzbek ones.

5 I'm sending you some photos of the camp. Love to all, and write soon!

Laylo
